report:
# Does standing at your desk help your health at the office?

**Verdict:** 📚 Published evidence only

## What the research and analysis found

The published evidence suggests that using a standing desk at work may help some aspects of office workers' health, but the answer is not a simple yes. Trials and reviews found that sit-stand desks reduce sitting time, with one trial reporting weekday sitting time decreased from 8.00 to 5.22 h/day (P = 0.03). [sbaab928c-effect] Several studies also report improvements in cardiometabolic markers, musculoskeletal discomfort, fatigue, and self-reported health, though some found no significant changes in self-reported health or cardiovascular risk. [s3d58221f-effect, s1932b0a3-effect, s70a86d27-effect, s1a666426-effect, s8cc6f7ca-effect, s0fac9fd2-effect, sbb65096a-effect] The sources describe a plausible path from standing desk use to less sitting time and then to overall health, but a plausible path does not show how big the effect is or that it happens.

## Question (PECO)

- **Population:** office workers who spend significant time sitting at a desk
- **Exposure:** using a standing desk for at least 2 hours per day during work hours
- **Comparator:** sitting at a traditional seated desk for the same duration
- **Outcome:** self-reported general health status, measured using standardized scales such as the SF-12 or similar, or objective measures like blood pressure, body mass index (BMI), and metabolic markers
- **Time window:** after 6 months of consistent use
- **Estimand:** ATE, mean difference, deviations handled as received

## Causal graph (DAG)

- standing_desk_use → overall_health: the question being tested
- standing_desk_use → sitting_time: cites sbaab928c-effect, s0dfa2536-effect, s6ff5b8ba-effect, s5187344f-effect
- sitting_time → overall_health: cites s88adcac9-effect, s42b29459-effect, s0d417161-effect
- standing_desk_use → energy_expenditure: cites s326d6387-effect, s474e85c8-effect, s868717eb-effect
- energy_expenditure → overall_health: assumed (no source)
- standing_desk_use → musculoskeletal_discomfort: cites s1932b0a3-effect, s1a666426-effect, s35e70dfe-effect, s5187344f-effect
- musculoskeletal_discomfort → overall_health: assumed (no source)
- age → overall_health: assumed (no source)
- sex → overall_health: assumed (no source)
- bmi → overall_health: assumed (no source)
- bmi → standing_desk_use: assumed (no source)
- job_tenure → standing_desk_use: assumed (no source)
- job_tenure → overall_health: assumed (no source)

Treated as exogenous (the model's judgment that nothing in the graph can cause it; no source): age, sex.

## Key confounders

- bmi
- job_tenure

## Evidence

**Certainty:** high (starts high: a trial or a review of trials matches)

Evidence flow: 113 sources found → 100 studies after dedupe → 64 included (excluded: wrong_outcome 10, not_a_study 4, wrong_exposure 18, off_topic 4).

Europe PMC lookups failed for 13 queries (after one retry): the studies they were for may lack a DOI or PMID and were not checked for retraction.

- [Providing office workers with height-adjustable workstation to reduce and interrupt workplace sitting time: protocol for the Stand Up for Healthy Aging (SUFHA) cluster randomized controlled trial.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10245479) — RCT, 2023: effect not verified
- [Effects of a Workplace Sit-Stand Desk Intervention on Health and Productivity.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8582919) — RCT, 2021: effect not verified
- [Ukumela impilo randomised trial: preliminary findings of height-adjustable sit-to-stand workstations on health outcomes of South African office workers.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10704807) — RCT, 2023: reducing sedentary behaviour and improving cardiometabolic outcomes in a cohort of South African office workers over a 3-month, follow-up period
- [Impact of Sit-Stand Desks on Subjective Sitting Time and Psychological Outcomes in Office Workers: Findings from the Stand Up for Healthy Ageing (SUFHA) Randomized Controlled Trial.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42010722) — RCT, 2026: weekday sitting time decreased from 8.00 to 5.22 h/day (P = 0.03)
- [Impact of sit-stand desks at work on energy expenditure, sitting time and cardio-metabolic risk factors: Multiphase feasibility study with randomised controlled component](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6603239) — RCT, 2019: increased standing time during waking hours of working days (60.7 min (−12.1, 133.5); decreased prolonged sitting time during waking hours of working days and during working hours (waking hours: −120.6 min (−355.2, 113.9); working hours: −100.2 min (−318.5, 118.0); and increased prolonged sitting time during non-working days, (>/30 min bouts: 249.6 min (−244.2, 743.4); >/60 min bouts: 241.1 min (−149.3, 631.5))

- [The effects of prolonged sitting, prolonged standing, and activity breaks on vascular function, and postprandial glucose and insulin responses: A randomised crossover trial.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7781669) — RCT, 2021: Prolonged Standing increased mean diastolic blood pressure by 8 mm Hg (95% CI 2 to 10 mm Hg; p = 0.006) when compared to Prolonged Sitting, and by 5 mm Hg (95% CI 1 to 8 mm Hg; p = 0.004) when compared to Regular Activity Breaks.
